chief_complaint: global loss of active and passive shoulder rotation, normal X-ray
hpi_details: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with global loss of active and passive shoulder rotation, normal x-ray. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he severely pulled a muscle or tore something in his shoulder from sleeping awkwardly or lifting weights.
concerns: He is worried that his shoulder is permanently frozen shut and that he will need invasive joint surgery.
expectations: He hopes to get a strong cortisone shot or prescription painkiller today so he can lift his arm to drive to work.

available_results.value: Preserved glenohumeral joint space without fracture, dislocation, calcific tendinopathy, or advanced osteoarthritis

clinical_knowledge.topic: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Management may include gentle, pain-limited range-of-motion exercises and physical therapy. Consider a glenohumeral corticosteroid injection only after diagnostic confirmation and assessment for contraindications.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: global loss of active and passive shoulder rotation, normal X-ray

Key HPI features: A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with global loss of active and passive shoulder rotation, normal x-ray. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Adhesive Capsulitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rotator cuff tear without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: fever, marked warmth or swelling, unexplained weight loss, or rapidly progressive weakness.
management_principles: Use gentle, pain-limited capsular stretching and consider physical therapy; avoid forceful manipulation.
Consider image-guided glenohumeral corticosteroid injection after confirmation and contraindication screening; refer for diagnostic uncertainty, severe pain, or failure of conservative management.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

red_flags: Fever, marked warmth, or swelling of the shoulder
Unexplained weight loss or rapidly progressive weakness

must_ask.objective: Active and passive range of motion
must_ask.say: Can you lift your arm yourself, or does it feel stiff even when someone tries to raise it for you?
Is it difficult to reach behind your back or comb your hair?
Does the shoulder pain wake you up at night when you lie on that side?
Do you have diabetes or thyroid conditions?
Did the pain start gradually before the stiffness set in?

history.answer: My right shoulder has become terribly stiff over the past few weeks, and now I can barely rotate or lift my arm at all.
It is only in my right shoulder. None of my other joints feel stiff or painful.
It started gradually about two months ago with a dull ache, but over the last few weeks the stiffness has steadily worsened.
It feels like a deep, persistent ache around four out of ten, but it shoots up to a sharp seven if I reach too far or bump against the movement limit.
No, there has not been any swelling, redness, or heat in the joint.
It feels quite stiff when I first get out of bed, but unlike arthritis, the stiffness does not loosen up after thirty minutes; it stays stiff all day.
Reaching overhead, putting on a jacket, or twisting my arm outward aggravates the pain. Resting it eases the ache, but the tightness never goes away.
I have trouble reaching into my back pocket, fastening my belt behind me, and washing my upper back. I can still use my right hand and fingers normally.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, I did not fall, twist the shoulder, or feel any pop or snap. It just began aching on its own.
No, I have never had any joint pain or shoulder stiffness like this before.
I have been feeling unusually run-down and fatigued lately, though I have not lost any weight.
No, I do not have any skin rashes, scalp flakes, mouth ulcers, or eye irritation.
No, my lower back feels fine in the morning, and I do not have any heel soreness or swollen digits.
No, I have not had any recent sore throat, stomach upset, diarrhea, or pain when urinating.
I eat an ordinary diet, do not consume large amounts of meat or seafood, and do not take water pills.
No, I have never had any steroid injections, shoulder operations, or artificial joint placements.
I am married and in a monogamous relationship, with no new sexual partners.
Even when I relax my arm completely and try to lift it with my good hand or have someone lift it for me, it hits a solid wall and will not move.
Yes, trying to rotate my right forearm outward away from my stomach is severely blocked and causes sharp pain.
Lying on my right side at night triggers a deep throbbing ache that often wakes me up from sleep.
I have never been diagnosed with diabetes, thyroid disorders, or had my arm immobilized in a sling or cast.
I was convinced I just pulled a muscle or tore something lifting at the gym, but it's so stiff now that I can't even reach to put my belt on.
I'm really scared that the joint is locked up for good and that I'm going to end up needing surgery.
I was hoping you could give me a cortisone shot or some strong painkillers today so I can at least drive myself to work.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions or long-standing illnesses.
I have never undergone surgery or been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked tobacco or used e-cigarettes.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps one or two glasses of beer over the weekend.
I work as an office manager doing mostly desk work, and I live with my wife.
Nobody in my family has a history of rheumatoid arthritis, gout, or chronic shoulder issues.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7°C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-nourished man sitting comfortably, holding the right arm slightly guarded against the torso without acute distress.

Right shoulder demonstrates marked restriction in both active and passive range of motion across all planes, most severely limiting external rotation and abduction, with pain at end-range; no erythema, warmth, joint effusion, or deformity.
Rotator cuff muscle strength testing is limited by capsular stiffness and end-range pain, but distal upper extremity strength is 5/5 bilaterally.
Intact sensation to light touch over bilateral axillary nerve distributions and upper extremities.
Biceps, triceps, and brachioradialis deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally.
Full and pain-free cervical spine range of motion without midline tenderness or radicular symptoms on Spurling maneuver.
No rashes, psoriatic plaques, subcutaneous tophi, or nail pitting observed.
